In mathematics, the '''Tate curve''' is a curve defined over the [[ring of formal power series]] <math>\mathbb{Z}[[q]]</math> with [[integer]] coefficients. Over the open subscheme where ''q'' is invertible, the Tate curve is an [[elliptic curve]].

The Tate curve can also be defined for ''q'' as an element of a [[complete field]] of norm less than 1, in which case the formal [[power series]] converge.

The Tate curve was introduced by {{harvs|txt|first=John |last=Tate|authorlink=John Tate (mathematician)|year=1995}} in a  1959 manuscript originally titled "Rational Points on Elliptic Curves Over Complete Fields"; he  did not publish his results until many years later, and his work first appeared in {{harvtxt|Roquette|1970}}.

==Definition==

The Tate curve is the [[projective plane]] curve over the ring  <math>\mathbb{Z}[[q]]</math> of formal power series with integer coefficients given (in an affine open subset of the projective plane) by the equation
:<math> y^2+xy=x^3+a_4x+a_6</math>
where
:<math>-a_4=5\sum_n \frac{n^3q^n}{1-q^n} = 5q+45q^2+140q^3+\cdots</math>
:<math>-a_6=\sum_{n}\frac{7n^5+5n^3}{12}\times\frac{q^n}{1-q^n} = q+23q^2+154q^3+\cdots</math>
are power series with integer coefficients.<ref>Manin & Panchishkin (2007) p.220</ref>

==The Tate curve over a complete field==

Suppose that the field <math>k</math> is complete with respect to some [[absolute value]] | |, and <math>q</math> is a non-zero element of the field <math>k</math> with <math>|q|<1</math>. Then the series above all converge, and define an elliptic curve over <math>k</math>. If in addition <math>q</math> is non-zero then there is an isomorphism of groups from <math>k^*/q^{\mathbb{Z}}</math> to this elliptic curve, taking <math>w</math> to <math>(x(w),y(w))</math> for <math>w</math> not a power of <math>q</math>, where
:<math>x(w)= -y(w)-y(w^{-1})</math>
:<math>y(w) = \sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}}\frac{(q^mw)^2}{(1-q^mw)^3} + \sum_{m \ge 1} \frac{q^m}{(1-q^m)^2}</math>
and taking powers of <math>q</math> to the point at infinity of the elliptic curve. The series <math>x(w)</math> and <math>y(w)</math> are not formal power series in <math>w</math>.

== Intuitive example ==

In the case of the curve over the complete field, <math>k^*/q^\mathbb{Z}</math>, the easiest case to visualize is <math>\mathbb{C}^*/q^\mathbb{Z}</math>, where <math>q^\mathbb{Z}</math> is the discrete subgroup generated by one multiplicative period <math> e^{2 \pi i \tau} </math>, where the period <math> \tau = \omega_1/\omega_2</math>. Note that <math>\mathbb{C}^*</math> is isomorphic to <math>{(\mathbb{C},+)}/ (\mathbb{Z},+)</math>, where <math>(\mathbb{C},+)</math> is the complex numbers under addition.

To see why the Tate curve morally corresponds to a torus when the field is <math>\mathbb{C}</math> with the usual norm, <math>q</math> is already singly periodic; modding out by <math>q</math>'s integral powers you are modding out <math>\mathbb{C}</math> by <math>\mathbb{Z}^2</math>, which is a torus. In other words, we have an annulus, and we glue inner and outer edges.

But the annulus does not correspond to the circle minus a point: the annulus is the set of complex numbers between two consecutive powers of <math>q</math>; say all complex numbers with magnitude between 1 and <math>q</math>. That gives us two circles, i.e., the inner and outer edges of an annulus.

The image of the torus given here is a bunch of inlaid circles getting narrower and narrower as they approach the origin.

This is slightly different from the usual method beginning with a flat sheet of paper, <math>\mathbb{C}</math>, and gluing together the sides to make a cylinder <math>\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{Z}</math>, and then gluing together the edges of the cylinder to make a torus, <math>\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{Z}^2</math>.

This is slightly oversimplified. The Tate curve is really a curve over a formal power series ring rather than a curve over C. Intuitively, it is a [[family of curves]] depending on a formal parameter. When that formal parameter is zero it degenerates to a pinched torus, and when it is nonzero it is a torus).

==Properties==
The [[j-invariant]] of the Tate curve is given by a power series in ''q'' with leading term ''q''<sup>−1</sup>.<ref>Silverman (1994) p.423</ref>  Over a ''p''-adic [[local field]], therefore, ''j'' is non-integral and the Tate curve has [[Semistable abelian variety|semistable reduction]] of multiplicative type.  Conversely, every semistable elliptic curve over a local field is isomorphic to a Tate curve (up to [[quadratic twist]]).<ref>Manin & Panchiskin (2007) p.300</ref>
